summary: Psalm 87 praises Zion as the city God loves and establishes. It begins with God's foundation in the holy mountains, then imagines nations being recorded as belonging there, and ends with singers and dancers saying that their springs are in Zion.
whyItMatters: This psalm sits in Book III of Psalms, where sanctuary, city, and the crisis of God's people are prominent concerns. Its unusual focus is not on Zion alone, but on peoples from beyond Israel being counted in relation to Zion.

context.author: Associated in the heading with the sons of Korah; Psalms headings may indicate authorship, association, collection, dedication, or performance setting, and their exact force is debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Individual psalms come from different periods, and the five-book Psalter is a later anthology; a single date for Psalm 87 cannot be established from this chapter alone.
context.setting: The poem is oriented toward Zion, the city of God, within the wider Psalms collection where many poems look toward Jerusalem and temple worship.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and public praise, with a heading, repeated birth-record language, and two occurrences of Selah as a preserved performance marker of uncertain exact meaning.

outline.heading: Zion's Loved Foundation
outline.note: The psalm names the holy mountains, the gates of Zion, and the city of God as the place Yahweh especially loves.

outline.heading: Nations Recorded With Zion
outline.note: Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia are named among peoples connected to Zion through the repeated declaration, “This one was born there.”

outline.heading: Singers at the Springs
outline.note: The psalm closes with singers and dancers saying that all their springs are in Zion.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.
keyVerses.why: This states the psalm's central preference: Zion is singled out as loved by Yahweh among Jacob's dwellings.

keyVerses.text: I will record Rahab and Babylon among those who acknowledge me. Behold, Philistia, Tyre, and also Ethiopia: “This one was born there.”
keyVerses.why: This is the poem's striking expansion, naming foreign peoples and places in connection with being recorded by God.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh will count, when he writes up the peoples, “This one was born there.” Selah.
keyVerses.why: This verse repeats the registration image and makes Yahweh the one who counts the peoples.

keyVerses.text: Those who sing as well as those who dance say, “All my springs are in you.”
keyVerses.why: The closing line turns the chapter's vision into public celebration and locates life-giving source imagery in Zion.

questions.question: What is Zion in this psalm?
questions.answer: In this chapter, Zion is the place whose gates Yahweh loves and the city addressed as the city of God. The psalm does not pause to explain its geography, but many psalms are oriented toward Jerusalem and its temple. Here Zion functions as the center of the poem's praise and as the place to which peoples are connected.

questions.question: Who are the sons of Korah?
questions.answer: The heading associates this psalm with the sons of Korah. Psalms contains collections and headings linked with several figures and groups, including the Korahites, but headings may mark authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. So the heading is important evidence for how the psalm was transmitted, but it does not settle every question about its first composition.

questions.question: What does Selah mean?
questions.answer: Selah appears at the end of verses 3 and 6. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker, often left untranslated because its exact instruction is no longer known. In this psalm, it appears after the praise of the city of God and after Yahweh's counting of the peoples.

questions.question: Why are Rahab and Babylon named?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says, “I will record Rahab and Babylon among those who acknowledge me.” The chapter itself presents them as peoples or powers included in God's record, alongside Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia. Rahab here is a symbolic name for Egypt, one of the powers included in this vision of belonging.

questions.question: Does the psalm say these foreign peoples are replacing Israel?
questions.answer: The psalm does not say that. It says Yahweh loves Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob, and then it names other peoples being recorded with the words, “This one was born there.” Readers differ over how broadly to read this vision, but the chapter's own movement joins Zion's special status with an unexpectedly wide registration of peoples.

questions.question: What does “This one was born there” mean?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in verses 4 and 6, and a similar statement appears in verse 5 about Zion. The psalm uses birth language for belonging: peoples are counted as having a connection to Zion. It does not explain the mechanism or timing of that belonging, so the safest reading is to notice the image without turning it into a detailed system.

questions.question: Who is speaking in verse 4?
questions.answer: Verse 4 begins, “I will record,” and verse 6 says Yahweh will count when he writes up the peoples. Because of that nearby explanation, many readers take the “I” of verse 4 as God's voice. The psalm does not add a speech label, so it is best to state the likely connection while noticing the poem's compressed style.

questions.question: What is the importance of the Most High establishing Zion?
questions.answer: Verse 5 says, “the Most High himself will establish her.” In the psalm's logic, Zion is not merely admired by singers; it is secured by God. That claim supports the repeated registration language, because the city to which peoples are linked is presented as established by the Most High.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader handle the final line about springs?
questions.answer: Verse 7 places the words on the lips of singers and dancers: “All my springs are in you.” The image suggests source and supply, but the chapter does not define the springs in a technical way. The main point is that the poem ends in celebration, with Zion named as the source to which the worshipers look.

glossary.def: The place whose gates Yahweh loves and the city at the center of the psalm's praise.
A preserved performance marker in Psalms; its exact ancient instruction is uncertain.
A name in verse 4 listed with Babylon among those God records; here it is a symbolic name applied to Egypt.
A title for God in verse 5, where the psalm says he will establish Zion.
